phonemes.desc: stressed first syllable; classical zeta was a true 'zd' cluster, as in English 'wisdom', not a modern 'z'
phi was an aspirated p (p + breath), not an f; upsilon was a rounded French-like 'u' [y]
short final -os; the r lightly trilled

pronunciation.approximation: 'ZDEH-phee-ros' — stress the first syllable; begin with the 'zd' of 'wisdom', and let the phi puff air like an English 'up-hill', not an 'f'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ζόφος (zophos), 'gloom, darkness; the dark quarter of the sky — the west' — the word's likely kin, naming the wind from the quarter it blows from

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: uncertain; Beekes flags the formation as possibly Pre-Greek rather than securely Indo-European

pronunciation.note: Tier-2 — Accent-Preserving. The restoration Zéphyros preserves the acute stress of Ζέφυρος on the first syllable, a feature plain ASCII loses; it carries no long-vowel mark, so a single preserved feature places the name in Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath of Spring
domains.subtitle: The West Wind, Gentlest of the Anemoi
domains.lead: Zéphyros is the west wind of the Greeks — the mildest of the four Anemoi, the breeze that loosens winter and calls up the flowers. Where Bóreas rages and Nótos drowns ships in rain, Zéphyros is the wind the poets loved: the steady, fruit-bearing breath that fans the orchards of the blessed and carries spring north into the human world.

symbols.name: Garland of Flowers
symbols.meaning: On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, Zéphyros is carved as a youth whose folded cloak spills blossoms — his spring-bearing nature made visible in stone.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: Like all the Anemoi, he is winged in Greek and Roman art; the winds fly, and their wings mark them as powers of the air rather than ordinary gods.

symbols.name: Swift Horses
symbols.meaning: By Pódargē the harpy he fathered Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal horses of Achilles — the wind's own speed given equine form.

symbols.name: The Swallow
symbols.meaning: The swallow's return was proverbially bound to the west wind's season; both were the first messengers that winter had broken.

symbols.name: Billowing Sail
symbols.meaning: A kind wind for sailors: steady, mild, and western — the breeze that fills canvas without violence and carries ships home.

symbols.name: Youthful Bloom
symbols.meaning: In art he appears as a beautiful, unbearded youth, a wind conceived not as a destroyer but as a lover — fitting the bridegroom of Chlōris.

mythology.lead: Zéphyros is a minor god with an outsized poetic life: born of Dawn, lover of flowers, father of the fastest horses ever to run. His myths are few but luminous — each one binds the west wind to speed, desire, and the returning spring.

myths.title: Son of Dawn and the Starry Sky
myths.text: In Theogony 378–380, Hesiod records that Eōs (Dawn) bore to Astraios, the starry dusk, the mighty winds: Zéphyros, Bóreas, and Nótos — 'a goddess lying in love with a god'. The genealogy is exact: the clearing west wind is the child of first light and the star-field, born at the seam where night opens into day.

myths.title: Father of Achilles's Horses
myths.text: In Iliad 16 (149–151), Patroklos harnesses Achilles's immortal pair, Xánthos and Bálios, 'whom Pódargē, the harpy swift of foot, bore to Zéphyros the west wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Ōkeanos'. A wind coupling with a storm-snatcher in a meadow: Homer makes the horses' supernatural speed a literal inheritance. It is Xánthos, this same wind-begotten colt, who later speaks with a human voice to foretell Achilles's death (Iliad 19, 404–417).

myths.title: The Abduction of Chlōris
myths.text: In Ovid's Fasti 5 (195–214), the goddess Flora tells her own story: 'I who am now called Flora was once Chlōris… Zéphyros saw me, desired me, and carried me off' — then made her his lawful wife and gave her dominion over every flower, so that in her garden 'it is always spring'. Hyginus (Fabulae) preserves the fruit of the union: their son Karpós, 'Fruit' itself, the harvest that follows blossom.

myths.title: The Breeze of the Blessed Orchards
myths.text: In Odyssey 7 (112–132), the garden of King Alkinoös on Scheria — fruit upon fruit, pear ripening on pear, never failing winter or summer — is kept in perpetual bearing because 'the breath of Zéphyros, ever blowing, causes some fruits to swell and others to ripen'. Homer needs no allegory here: the west wind simply is the climate of paradise, the mildest air imaginable, made divine.

lore.syncretism: The Romans called him Favōnius, from favēre, 'to favor' — the propitious wind — and married him to their own flower-goddess Flōra, whose festival, the Floralia, kept the Greek Chlōris-marriage alive in cult. Horace (Odes 1.4) sings winter loosening 'under the welcome west wind', and Virgil lets Favonius breathe through the Georgics as the air that unbinds the fields. Through Latin poetry the name passed intact into every European vernacular: the gentle west wind of Greece became the zephyr of the modern world.
lore.culturalLegacy: English zephyr — 'a soft, gentle breeze' — descends directly from his name through Latin zephyrus, and has been a staple of English verse since Chaucer opened the Canterbury Tales with 'Zephirus… with his sweete breeth' quickening the spring crops. The word also gave its name to a fine, light yarn and to anything featherweight. Few Greek wind-gods survive so completely: not as a character, but as the very word English reaches for when the air turns kind.
lore.extendedMeditation: The Greeks did not usually worship the winds with temples and myths of their own — they felt them, and feeling was enough. Zéphyros is the clearest case of a natural force crossing into personality precisely because it was pleasant: the storm winds stay brute daimones, but the wind that opens the flowers earned a wife, a marriage bed, and children. His ambivalence is quiet but real — the same wind that breeds Achilles's immortal horses also breeds the speed that carries the hero toward death. For the Greeks the west wind was proof that the divine could be gentle without ceasing to be power: a daimon you pray to by opening the orchard gate.
lore.archaeology: Zéphyros's most famous monument is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestēs, 1st c. BCE) in the Roman Agora of Athens, whose octagonal frieze personifies the eight winds — Zéphyros on the west face as a youth scattering flowers from his folded cloak. Pausanias (2.12.1) records a sanctuary with an altar of the Winds at Titanē in Sikyonia, where a priest sacrificed to them annually — one of the few attested cult sites for the Anemoi as a group. In Rome, his cult life ran through his bride: the temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and the games of the Floralia.
